newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan April current account surplus.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan April current account surplus.

text.p: The following is a selection of economists' and analysts' initial reaction to Japan's current account data for April, which the government said on Wednesday jumped 92.7 percent to 1.09 trillion yen.
MASANOBU TAKAHASHI, DIRECTOR AND HEAD OF RESEARCH AT SANYO INVESTMENT RESEARCH
"A more than one trillion yen surplus for trade and the current account was expected by most observers. Actually, it was not a big surprise."

"The change in psychology in the currency market is that there is now more of an emphasis on these numbers," Takahashi said, adding that foreign exchange market participants are looking more at trade figures now, rather than industrial production data.
With the announcement of customs-cleared trade figures for May soon, "For some time from now, these will push the yen stronger against the dollar."
RICHARD JERRAM, CHIEF ECONOMIST ING BARING SECURITIES:

"People are interested not so much in the April numbers but in the May figures for customs-cleared trade, which will show the surplus more than doubled. So these figures are not a one-off fluke, it's the beginning of a trend of a strongly rising surplus."
ANDREW SHIPLEY, ECONOMIST AT SCHRODERS JAPAN LTD

"Certainly concern in the market has heightened regarding trade friction... the surge in April in the trade surplus has sparked fears that the U.S. will start protesting attempts by Japan to export its way of the slowdown."

"But there are some seasonal factors at work here as well. We had a consumption tax hike the same month which dramatically depressed import growth, which is one of the major reasons behind the growth in the trade surplus."

"In addition, the U.S. economy is going gangbusters at present...now if it doesn't slow of its own accord, then the Fed will be forced to move and as a result there is a very high probability that the U.S. economy is going to be slowing in the second half of the year, decreasing demand for Japanese exports -- the point being that we see the increase in the surplus as a temporary development, certainly to end by the first half of the current fiscal year."

"I don't think it's really fair to analyse April data. A great deal of trade shipments is focused at the end of the fiscal year in March and also at the end of interim period in September. In fact, we see a sharp drop-off in trade flows in April. It is not really representative of overall trade patterns."

"We had a consumption tax hike in the same month which had a dramatic depressing impact on imports. We've already seen in May evidence of imports rebounding -- they're up 12 percent, the first 20 day figures."

Shipley, speaking to Reuters Financial Television (RFTV), said that he did not see the danger that the ratio of the current account surplus against the gross domestic product will approach the 2.5 percent level this year.
"The main reason for export strength right now is the surging growth in the U.S. But the U.S. economy will be slowing from the breakneck pace it's recording now."
"We'll see export growth declining. At the same time, imports are poised to rebound on the back of inventory re-stocking.

"We see current account surplus resuming its long-term trend downwards from the second half of the year on the back of slowing overseas demand and resumption of economic growth following fiscal tightening".

Takahashi, who was also speaking to RFTV, said, "There are rumours that Japanese trade will be at the top of the agenda at the Denver summit, but no other members are really concerned about the Japanese trade numbers except for the U.S."
